prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube (B054) and still regard it as a major achievement, but after reading the eight ballots I think B057 is the stronger prize case. Magic-wavelength trapping is a concrete invention with an unambiguous measurable outcome: many neutral atoms interrogated in parallel at fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, reproduced independently by several national laboratories and routinely compared between them. It has enabled tests of relativity and of constant variation, relativistic geodesy and a credible path to redefining the second. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori proposed and first realised the lattice concept, and Ye's group drove it to record accuracy and stability. Two names fit the three-person limit without hard exclusions, and as an instrument builder I value a prize where the instrument and the physics are inseparable.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier recognition: the frequency comb (Hall and Hansch, 2005) and ion-trap and single-quantum-system work (2012) already sit behind optical clocks, and Ye's programme is bound up with comb-linked comparisons. The committee may see lattice clocks as a family of incremental advances in a long precision-measurement tradition rather than a single discovery, and other lattice-clock and ion-clock groups are not in the credited names. Practical consequences, such as the redefinition of the second, are still pending. A fair alternative reading is that the larger open question in the field is a new observational window, which is what B054 offers.

responses.point: B057 is a clear discovery-plus-invention with a compact two-name credit and stable, independently confirmed interpretation, ranked first despite possible overlap with comb and ion-clock traditions.
responses.response: I agree with the core argument and have moved toward it. My one qualification is the overlap you flag: I think it is answerable, because the 2005 prize rewarded the comb as a frequency-measurement tool and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single quantum systems, whereas magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms is a distinct idea whose point is to remove motional and light-shift errors while keeping statistical power. The citation should therefore name the lattice mechanism explicitly rather than optical clocks generally.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B026 (room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance) first as a compact, consequential discovery with well-understood physics and large commercial use, but notes it is adjacent to the 2007 giant magnetoresistance prize and ranks B057 fourth because of the 2005 comb overlap.
responses.response: I take the B026 case seriously and see its clean experimental origin in 1995, but I disagree that it is the strongest candidate. The 2007 prize already recognised spin-dependent transport in magnetic multilayers and its read-head application, so B026 has to argue novelty on a refinement, and the credit among Miyazaki, Moodera and Parkin includes later MgO-barrier optimisation that is more engineering than discovery. On the 2005 overlap I think B057 is better protected: the scientific outcome (1e-18 clocks with magic-wavelength trapping) is new, whereas the TMR story is a continuation of a recognised line. I would keep B026 off my alternatives only because other candidates seem to me to have broader reach.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the cavity method and statistical-physics inference (B025) first, as a controlled framework for constraint satisfaction, coding and inference with rigorous confirmation, noting that its origins lie with Parisi, already a laureate.
responses.response: I respect the conceptual weight of B025 and the point about mathematical confirmation, but I disagree with ranking it above experimentally anchored candidates. Its roots in replica and cavity methods were recognised in 2021, so a new prize must isolate the finite-connectivity and survey-propagation contributions of Mezard and Zecchina as a distinct discovery, and the credit then sits uneasily with Montanari's more mathematical contribution. Its impact is large but largely on computer science and statistics, which makes the physics-prize framing the contested step. I would want the committee to see that argument made before preferring it to a measured, reproduced physical effect.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B057 first, calls the concept original and clean, and ranks B053 (topological insulators) second as overdue rather than premature, with B015 third.
responses.response: I agree with you on B057 and its timing. On B053 I agree it is mature and well confirmed, but I think the credit problem is more serious than your ballot suggests: Kane-Mele and Molenkamp is a defensible core, yet the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that the HgTe experiment tested and Hasan's three-dimensional work are both excluded or contested, and the 2016 prize already covered topological phases of matter. That is why I keep B053 as an alternative rather than my preferred option.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron microscopy (B048) first as a true invention, with a natural Rose-Haider-Urban trio and overdue maturity, and B057 second.
responses.response: As someone who builds instruments I am sympathetic: B048 is exactly the kind of invention-driven advance the Nobel statutes favour, and the three names are well matched to theory, implementation and demonstration. My reservation is that its impact is as an enabling tool for other science, with Krivanek's STEM-side work outside the credit, whereas B057 delivers a measured fundamental result, a 10^-18 frequency standard that tests physics directly. If the committee prefers a pure instrumentation prize, B048 deserves a proper hearing, but the opening support does not put it in contention with B057.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads lattice clocks as one distinct achievement or as a continuation of the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes.
Whether IceCube (B054) should be preferred if the committee values opening a new observational window over metrological precision, given that source-level associations remain of modest significance.
Whether other lattice-clock contributors beyond Katori and Ye should be acknowledged in the citation wording, as I cannot verify the detailed credit split.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B057, whose field (atomic clocks) is far from my own. For B054 (IceCube), I note only a field-adjacent connection: I work in astroparticle physics and am a co-author in the Fermi-LAT collaboration, a gamma-ray instrument paper author. My profile records no tie to the credited names or to IceCube, so I see no recusal need, but I disclose the proximity.
